meta.title: Nephrology Literature Update
meta.query: Clinical nephrology — RCTs, systematic reviews & meta-analyses (humans, English)
meta.source: PubMed (NLM) abstracts; summaries and appraisals generated automatically from those abstracts. Each entry links to its PubMed record and DOI.
meta.note: Summaries and PICO are machine analyses of the source abstracts; criteria marked “not specified” were not stated. Read the source before acting clinically.

articles.authors: Zhang Y, Xing J, Wang GX, Chen YB, Mao DD
articles.title: Effects of E-Coach-Based Chronic Disease Management on Self-Management, Quality of Life, and Mental Health in Maintenance Hemodialysis Patients.
articles.summary: In an RCT of 96 maintenance hemodialysis patients, adding a 6-month WeChat-based E-Coach intervention to usual care significantly improved self-management behavior scores compared with usual care alone (ANCOVA F(1, 93) = 6.3, p = 0.014, partial η2 = 0.06; mean difference +11.6, 95% CI: 9.7 to 13.6, p < 0.001). The E-Coach group showed a between-group difference in change of +13.3 points (95% CI: 9.9 to 16.5), as well as improvements in KDQOL-SF, reductions in SDS and SAS scores, and lower serum potassium and phosphorus levels at 6 months.

pico.intervention: Usual care plus WeChat-based E-Coach mini-application providing education, dietary/exercise guidance, medication reminders, and online counseling
pico.outcome: Self-management behavior score at 6 months (primary); secondary outcomes included Kidney Disease Quality of Life-Short Form (KDQOL-SF), Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS), Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS), and serum potassium and phosphorus levels

appraisal.bottom_line: A WeChat-based E-Coach intervention added to usual care improved self-management behavior scores by a mean difference of +11.6 points (95% CI: 9.7 to 13.6; p < 0.001) over 6 months compared with usual care alone, alongside improvements in reported quality of life, anxiety, depression, and lower serum potassium and phosphorus levels.
appraisal.relevance: Digital health tools delivered through mobile applications may offer a practical, low-cost approach to enhance patient self-management, dietary compliance, and psychological well-being in maintenance hemodialysis patients.
appraisal.caveat: The small sample size (n = 96) from a single region limits generalizability, and blinding of participants to digital health coaching is impossible, introducing potential performance and reporting bias for subjective questionnaire outcomes.

articles.authors: Vázquez-Lorente H, Plaza-Diaz J, Pérez-Acosta JA, Díaz-López A, Salas-Salvadó J
articles.title: Nut Consumption, Kidney Function, Chronic Kidney Disease and Mortality: A Systematic Review.
articles.summary: This systematic review of observational studies evaluated the association between nut consumption and kidney health. Higher nut intake and replacing red and processed meats with nuts were associated with lower CKD risk or prevalence in certain populations. Findings for eGFR and albuminuria were inconsistent, evidence in established CKD populations was limited, and study heterogeneity prevented meta-analytic pooling.

pico.population: General populations and individuals evaluated for kidney health outcomes or CKD
pico.intervention: Higher nut intake or substitution of red and processed meats with nuts
pico.comparison: Lower nut intake or non-substitution of red/processed meat
pico.outcome: CKD incidence and prevalence, mortality, eGFR, and albuminuria

inclusion: Observational studies and cohort analyses evaluating nut intake and kidney health outcomes

appraisal.bottom_line: Higher nut intake and replacing red or processed meats with nuts are observational correlates of lower CKD risk in some cohorts, but effects on specific markers like eGFR and albuminuria are inconsistent.
appraisal.relevance: Plant-focused dietary strategies that substitute nuts for processed red meats align with broader cardiorenal disease management guidelines, though specific target intakes for CKD patients remain unproven.
appraisal.caveat: The underlying literature consists entirely of observational studies with substantial heterogeneity in exposure definitions and population characteristics; observational associations must not be interpreted as causal proof that nut consumption prevents CKD progression.

articles.authors: Lasa-Berasain P, Torrecilla Ugarte A, Juárez-Vela R, Ibánez-Beróiz B, Ansotegui Hernández A et al.
articles.title: Clinical prediction models in cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical prediction models (CPMs) for cardiac surgery-associated AKI (CSA-AKI) in adults undergoing cardiopulmonary bypass found a pooled CSA-AKI incidence of 26.3% (95% CI: 26.0-26.4%) and a CSA-AKI requiring RRT (CSA-AKI RRT) rate of 2.2% (95% CI: 2.1-2.2%). The Thakar 2005 model demonstrated the best predictive performance for CSA-AKI RRT with a pooled AUC of 0.80 (95% CI: 0.77-0.82), sensitivity 0.87, and specificity 0.49 at threshold >=3, though calibration showed risk underestimation.

pico.population: Adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass
pico.intervention: Clinical prediction models (CPMs) for CSA-AKI (e.g., Thakar 2005, Mehta 2006, Wijeysundera 2007, Demirjian 2022)
pico.comparison: Observed clinical incidence of CSA-AKI or CSA-AKI requiring dialysis
pico.outcome: Model discrimination (AUC, sensitivity, specificity) and calibration for CSA-AKI and CSA-AKI requiring RRT

inclusion: Studies developing or validating clinical prediction models for CSA-AKI in adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass

appraisal.bottom_line: Existing clinical prediction models, particularly the Thakar 2005 model (pooled AUC 0.80, 95% CI: 0.77-0.82), perform reasonably well for discriminating patients at risk for CSA-AKI requiring dialysis, though performance for milder stages of AKI remains poorer and calibration frequently underestimates risk.
appraisal.relevance: Risk stratification tools can assist clinicians in identifying high-risk cardiac surgery candidates who might benefit from targeted perioperative renal protection pathways.
appraisal.caveat: Most older models lack discrimination for milder stage 1-2 AKI and consistently suffer from calibration drift (underestimating risk) when applied across contemporary surgical cohorts.

articles.authors: Caetano AFP, Oliveira JA, Silva AWD, Cabral Junior CR, Cavalcante MJO et al.
articles.title: Effects of muscle strength training with blood flow restriction on glomerular function in people with stage 3 chronic kidney disease.
articles.summary: In a 12-week randomized trial of 40 patients with stage 3 CKD, low-load muscle strength training combined with blood flow restriction (MST+BFR, G4) was compared to control (G1), low-load MST (G2), and high-load MST (G3). G4 demonstrated a significant increase in albuminuria (p = 0.048) and significant differences in serum creatinine compared with G1 (p = 0.032) and G2 (p = 0.036), as well as eGFR-Cr compared with G2 (p = 0.032).

pico.population: Patients with stage 3 chronic kidney disease (n = 40)
pico.intervention: Low-load muscle strength training combined with blood flow restriction (MST+BFR; Group 4)
pico.comparison: Control (G1), low-load MST alone (G2), and high-load MST alone (G3)
pico.outcome: Glomerular function markers including serum creatinine, cystatin C, eGFR-Cr, and urinary microalbuminuria over 12 weeks

inclusion: Individuals with stage 3 chronic kidney disease

appraisal.bottom_line: Combining blood flow restriction with low-load resistance training in stage 3 CKD patients resulted in a statistically significant increase in albuminuria (p = 0.048) and changes in serum creatinine compared to controls without acute major renal toxicity.
appraisal.relevance: Blood flow restriction training is gaining interest in rehabilitation, but its acute hemodynamic effects may transiently worsen albuminuria in patients with pre-existing impaired renal function.
appraisal.caveat: The trial is severely limited by a very small sample size (10 patients per arm across 4 groups), making it underpowered for clinical endpoints and prone to baseline imbalances or false-positive findings.

articles.authors: Otabir SAG, Tegegne TK, Nderitu P, Wang J, Shaw JE et al.
articles.title: Detection and Risk Prediction of Diabetes Related Kidney Disease Using Retinal Images: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of deep learning models for detecting and predicting diabetes-related kidney disease (DRKD) using retinal images included 6 studies. A meta-analysis of 3 cross-sectional hybrid model studies showed a pooled AUC of 0.88, sensitivity of 0.80, and specificity of 0.81, though heterogeneity was high (I2 = 93.7%-99.8%). Hybrid models combining retinal images and clinical data outperformed retinal-image-only models (delta AUC 0.03-0.11).

pico.population: Patients with diabetes mellitus evaluated for diabetes-related kidney disease (DRKD)
pico.intervention: Deep learning models utilizing 2D retinal images alone or hybrid models combining retinal images with clinical data
pico.comparison: Clinical-data-only prediction models or retinal-image-only models
pico.outcome: Model diagnostic and predictive performance (AUC, sensitivity, specificity)

inclusion: Cross-sectional and longitudinal studies evaluating deep learning models for DRKD detection or prediction using retinal images alone, clinical data alone, or hybrid models

appraisal.bottom_line: Deep learning hybrid models incorporating retinal images and clinical data detect DRKD with an overall pooled AUC of 0.88 (sensitivity 0.80, specificity 0.81), outperforming retinal images alone by a delta AUC of 0.03 to 0.11.
appraisal.relevance: Ophthalmologic screening programs for diabetic retinopathy could theoretically dual-screen for early diabetic kidney disease without requiring extra patient procedures.
appraisal.caveat: Only 6 studies met inclusion criteria with massive statistical heterogeneity (I2 > 93%), and only a single longitudinal study evaluated future risk prediction (5-year AUC 0.81), limiting generalizability.

articles.authors: Neo HLM, Naidu KNC, Tang IJH, Tiong HY, Goh SYS et al.
articles.title: Psychological factors associated with medication non-adherence after kidney transplant: a systematic review.
articles.summary: A systematic review of 44 quantitative and qualitative studies comprising 11,180 adult kidney transplant recipients found self-reported medication non-adherence prevalence ranging from 12.0% to 89.2%. Depressive symptoms and low social support were the most consistent psychological correlates, alongside qualitative barriers such as emotional burden, stigma, and regimen complexity.

pico.population: Adult kidney transplant recipients (n = 11,180 across 44 studies)
pico.intervention: Presence of psychological factors (depressive symptoms, low social support, emotional distress, stigma)
pico.comparison: Absence or lower severity of adverse psychological factors

inclusion: Quantitative and qualitative studies involving adult kidney transplant recipients evaluating psychological factors associated with self-reported medication non-adherence

appraisal.bottom_line: Across 44 studies, self-reported non-adherence ranged wildly from 12.0% to 89.2%, with depressive symptoms and lack of social support identified as the strongest and most consistent correlates.
appraisal.relevance: Post-transplant medication adherence is critical for graft survival; identifying depressive symptoms and weak social support systems offers actionable targets for clinical intervention.
appraisal.caveat: The wide variance in non-adherence prevalence (12% to 89%) reflects significant heterogeneity in self-reported measurement tools, which are inherently prone to recall and social desirability biases.

articles.authors: Karimi R, Riahi R, Mortazavi M, Sindarreh S, Aminorroaya A et al.
articles.title: Association between prediabetes and nephropathy: a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 26 studies (350,546 normal glucose tolerance controls, 146,547 prediabetes subjects) evaluated the association between prediabetes and nephropathy. Prediabetes was associated with increased CKD risk (19 studies: RR 1.53, 95% CI: 1.30-1.81, p < 0.001), a reduction in eGFR across 31 observations (MD: -2.85 mL/min/1.73m2, 95% CI: -4.57 to -1.13, p = 0.001), and higher UACR across 21 observations (MD: 0.87, 95% CI: 0.19-1.55, p = 0.012).

pico.population: Individuals with prediabetes versus normal glucose tolerance (total n = 497,093)
pico.outcome: Incident or prevalent chronic kidney disease risk (RR), mean difference in eGFR, and mean difference in urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR)

inclusion: Cohort and cross-sectional studies published before November 2024 evaluating prediabetes and nephropathy outcomes compared to normal glucose tolerance

appraisal.bottom_line: Prediabetes is significantly associated with increased risk of chronic kidney disease (RR 1.53, 95% CI: 1.30-1.81, p < 0.001), a modest lower mean eGFR (-2.85 mL/min/1.73m2), and higher UACR (+0.87).
appraisal.relevance: Renal microvascular end-organ damage begins before clinical diagnostic thresholds for overt type 2 diabetes mellitus are crossed, reinforcing the importance of metabolic control in prediabetes.
appraisal.caveat: The meta-analysis combines cross-sectional and prospective cohort designs, meaning the observed associations cannot establish direct causality or rule out residual confounding by hypertension and metabolic syndrome.

articles.authors: Bellos I, Marinaki S, Benetou V
articles.title: Lipoprotein(a) and adverse cardiovascular outcomes in dialysis patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 reports (14 cohorts, 6,380 maintenance dialysis patients) evaluated circulating Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] levels and outcomes. Exploratory meta-analyses showed elevated Lp(a) levels were associated with higher all-cause mortality (HR: 1.58, 95% CI: 1.24-2.02), cardiovascular mortality (HR: 2.07, 95% CI: 1.22-3.50), and MACE (HR: 1.56, 95% CI: 1.28-1.90), though certainty of evidence was rated low to very low.

pico.population: Maintenance hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis patients (n = 6,380 across 14 cohorts)
pico.outcome: All-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE)

inclusion: Observational cohort studies evaluating circulating Lp(a) levels and adverse CV outcomes in maintenance dialysis patients

appraisal.bottom_line: Elevated Lp(a) in maintenance dialysis patients is associated with increased all-cause mortality (HR 1.58, 95% CI: 1.24-2.02), CV mortality (HR 2.07, 95% CI: 1.22-3.50), and MACE (HR 1.56, 95% CI: 1.28-1.90), but evidence certainty is low to very low.
appraisal.relevance: Lp(a) represents a potential novel non-traditional cardiovascular biomarker in ESRD, where traditional risk factors fail to fully explain high cardiovascular event rates.
appraisal.caveat: The observational pooled estimates are considered exploratory due to low sample sizes, lack of assay standardization across studies, undefined clinical cutoff thresholds, and low certainty of evidence.
